## Answer Key: Chapter 1 {#sec-solutions-ch1 .unnumbered}

Full solutions to Chapter 1's "Check your understanding" questions
(@sec-ch1).

**1. Quick check. Two ablation runs use different tokenizers. Can their
training-loss curves be compared directly to decide which run is
better?**

*Answer.* No. Different tokenizers split the same text into a
different number of pieces, so the two loss numbers are not measuring
the same quantity — a lower loss under one tokenizer does not mean the
underlying model is better than one trained with a different
tokenizer.

*Common trap:* Treating "lower loss" as a universal, tokenizer-
independent scoreboard. It is only comparable across runs that share
the same tokenizer.

**2. Calculation. A team allocates a 50-billion-token budget across
three sources with mixing weights 0.6, 0.3, and 0.1. How many tokens
does each source receive?**

*Answer.* Source 1: $0.6 \times 50\text{B} = 30\text{B}$ tokens.
Source 2: $0.3 \times 50\text{B} = 15\text{B}$ tokens. Source 3:
$0.1 \times 50\text{B} = 5\text{B}$ tokens. Check: $30\text{B} +
15\text{B} + 5\text{B} = 50\text{B}$, matching the total budget.

**3. Misconception check. True or false: training only on the
highest-quality-seeming subset of available text (discarding
everything else) is always the best strategy for a model with a large
token budget.**

*Answer.* False. For a large token budget, discarding most available
data forces heavy repetition of the remaining small pool, and reported
prior work found that this kind of repetition can hurt performance —
so the highest-quality subset alone is not automatically the best
training set once repetition costs are accounted for.

**4. Explain. An architecture ablation shows a small improvement at
small scale, and a separate ablation shows a small regression at small
scale. Which of the two results should a team trust with less
additional testing, and why?**

*Answer.* The regression (negative result). The chapter's source
reports that if a change hurts performance at small scale, that result
can be confidently ruled out at large scale without further testing —
but a small-scale improvement needs more tokens trained before a team
can be confident it will hold at full scale, since positive results
are the weaker signal of the two.

*Common trap:* Treating both a small positive and a small negative
result as equally strong evidence, when the chapter's source reports
an explicit asymmetry between them.

**5. Compare. State one concrete reason a team might prefer a
multi-stage (curriculum) data mixture over a single fixed mixture for
the whole training run.**

*Answer.* Any one of: (a) a model's final behavior is disproportionately
shaped by data seen late in training, so reserving small, high-quality
sources for a late "annealing" stage can have more impact than mixing
them in from the start at a diluted ratio; (b) a fixed mixture cannot
respond to a capability bottleneck discovered partway through training,
while a multi-stage mixture can introduce targeted data once a
bottleneck (e.g. plateauing math performance) is observed.
